notes.definition: Acids produce hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solution and alkalis produce hydroxide ions (OH⁻). The pH scale, from 0 to 14, measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, and in neutralisation hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to form water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
explanation: When an acid dissolves in water it produces hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq). For example, hydrochloric acid gives H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and sulfuric acid gives H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions. It is the hydrogen ions that make a solution acidic. Alkalis are soluble bases; in aqueous solution they produce hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq). For example, sodium hydroxide solution contains Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions. It is the hydroxide ions that make a solution alkaline.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution. A solution with pH 7 is neutral, like pure water. Acidic solutions have pH values less than 7, and the lower the pH, the more acidic the solution. Alkaline solutions have pH values greater than 7, and the higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution. For example, stomach acid has a pH of about 1 to 2, vinegar about 3, pure water 7, soap about 9 to 10 and oven cleaner about 13.

Universal indicator is a wide range indicator: a mixture of dyes that turns a different colour at different pH values. To use it, add a few drops to the solution (or dip universal indicator paper into it) and compare the colour with a pH colour chart. Typical colours are red for strong acids (pH 0 to 2), orange and yellow for weak acids (pH 3 to 6), green for neutral (pH 7), blue for weak alkalis (pH 8 to 10) and purple for strong alkalis (pH 11 to 14). Universal indicator only gives an approximate pH, usually to the nearest whole number, and judging colours can vary between people.

A pH probe connected to a pH meter or data logger measures pH electronically. It gives a numerical reading, often to one or two decimal places, so it is more precise than universal indicator and does not depend on judging a colour. It can also record pH continuously, which is useful when following a neutralisation reaction. The probe must be calibrated using buffer solutions of known pH and rinsed with distilled water between samples.

In a neutralisation reaction between an acid and an alkali, the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the alkali to produce water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). The other ions, such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ when sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid, do not change; they stay in solution as the salt. This is why every acid and alkali neutralisation has the same ionic equation. If alkali is added gradually to an acid, the pH rises slowly at first, then very quickly through pH 7 when the amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻ are equal, and then levels off at a high pH when the alkali is in excess.
keyFacts: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq), in aqueous solution.
Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq).
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14.
pH 7 is neutral; pH less than 7 is acidic; pH greater than 7 is alkaline.
The lower the pH, the more acidic; the higher the pH, the more alkaline.
pH can be measured with universal indicator (approximate) or a pH probe (more precise).
Universal indicator: red (strong acid), orange/yellow (weak acid), green (neutral), blue (weak alkali), purple (strong alkali).
Neutralisation of an acid by an alkali: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
The other ions in an acid and alkali reaction stay in solution and form the salt.

keyTerms.definition: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
Neither acidic nor alkaline; a neutral solution has pH 7.
A substance that produces hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solution; its solution has a pH below 7.
A soluble base whose aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻, and has a pH above 7.
A wide range indicator that shows a range of colours to give the approximate pH of a solution.
An electronic sensor used with a meter or data logger to measure pH precisely as a number.
The reaction between an acid and a base or alkali; for acids and alkalis, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

workedExamples.title: Reading pH data from a neutralisation
workedExamples.question:
Sodium hydroxide solution was added to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid and the pH measured with a probe:
Volume of NaOH (cm³): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
pH: 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 7.0, 12.0, 12.3
State the volume of alkali needed to neutralise the acid and the overall change in pH.
steps: Neutral means pH 7. The pH is 7.0 when 20 cm³ of sodium hydroxide has been added.
The starting pH is 1.0 and the final pH is 12.3.
Notice the big jump between 15 cm³ and 25 cm³: this is where the H⁺ ions run out.

workedExamples.title: Scaling up a neutralisation
workedExamples.question: 25 cm³ of an acid is neutralised by 20 cm³ of an alkali. What volume of the same alkali is needed to neutralise 60 cm³ of the same acid?
steps: The volume of alkali needed is proportional to the volume of acid.
Alkali per cm³ of acid = 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8 cm³.

workedExamples.title: Identifying solutions from indicator colours
workedExamples.question: Universal indicator was added to three solutions. A turned purple, B turned green and C turned orange. Give an approximate pH for each and say whether it is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
steps: Purple shows a strong alkali: pH about 12 to 14, alkaline.
Orange shows a weak acid: pH about 3 to 4, acidic.
workedExamples.answer: A: about pH 13, alkaline. B: pH 7, neutral. C: about pH 3 to 4, acidic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a higher pH means a stronger acid.
misconceptions.right: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution. pH 1 is much more acidic than pH 5.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think neutralisation means the solution always ends up at exactly pH 7.
misconceptions.right: The solution is only neutral (pH 7) when exactly the right amounts react. Too much alkali gives a pH above 7, too little leaves it below 7.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think universal indicator gives an exact pH value.
misconceptions.right: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH (to about the nearest whole number). A pH probe gives a more precise reading.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all the ions react in neutralisation.
misconceptions.right: Only H⁺ and OH⁻ react to form water. The metal ions and the negative ions from the acid stay in solution as the salt.

realWorld: Gardeners test soil pH with universal indicator kits and add lime to acidic soils, because many crops grow best near pH 6 to 7.
Swimming pool water is kept at about pH 7.2 to 7.6 using pH test kits or probes, so it does not irritate swimmers' eyes.
Antacid tablets raise the pH in the stomach by neutralising excess hydrochloric acid.
Toothpaste is slightly alkaline, helping to neutralise acids made by bacteria in the mouth that can damage tooth enamel.
examTips: Learn the three key points: pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic (H⁺), above 7 alkaline (OH⁻).
When describing how to use universal indicator, mention comparing the colour with a pH colour chart.
Learn the ionic equation H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) with state symbols; it is the same for every acid and alkali.
If asked why a pH probe is better, say it gives a numerical, more precise value and does not depend on judging a colour.
When reading pH data, look for the volume where pH = 7 and describe the sudden change in pH around the neutral point.
summary: Acids produce H⁺ ions in water; alkalis produce OH⁻ ions.
pH scale 0 to 14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
Measure pH with universal indicator (approximate) or a pH probe (precise).
The other ions stay in solution and form the salt.
Adding alkali to acid raises the pH, with a rapid change around pH 7.

flashcards.front: Which ions do acids produce in aqueous solution?
Which ions are in aqueous solutions of alkalis?
What is the range of the pH scale?
Universal indicator colour in a neutral solution
Universal indicator colour in a strong acid and in a strong alkali
flashcards.back: Red in a strong acid; purple in a strong alkali.
Universal indicator (solution or paper) and a pH probe/meter.

flashcards.front: Why is a pH probe better than universal indicator?
flashcards.back: It gives a precise numerical reading and does not rely on judging colour.

questions.question: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: 7
questions.explanation: pH 7 is neutral. pH 0 and 1 are strongly acidic, and pH 14 is strongly alkaline.

questions.question: Which ion do all acids produce in aqueous solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺
questions.explanation: Hydrogen ions make solutions acidic. Hydroxide ions (OH⁻) are found in alkalis. Cl⁻ only comes from hydrochloric acid, not all acids.

questions.question: Which ion is present in all aqueous solutions of alkalis?
markScheme: 1 mark: OH⁻
questions.explanation: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions, OH⁻, in water. Na⁺ is only present in sodium hydroxide, not all alkalis.

questions.question: A solution has a pH of 2. How would you describe it?
markScheme: 1 mark: strongly acidic
questions.explanation: pH 2 is far below 7, so the solution is strongly acidic. Weakly acidic solutions are around pH 4 to 6.

questions.question: What colour does universal indicator turn in a neutral solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: green
questions.explanation: Green shows pH 7. Red shows a strong acid, yellow a weak acid and purple a strong alkali.

questions.question: Which equation represents the reaction that happens in every neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxide ions from the alkali to make water. The salt ions stay dissolved. The third equation forms hydrogen gas, which happens with metals, not alkalis.

questions.question: Which pH value shows the most alkaline solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: 13
questions.explanation: Above 7 is alkaline, and the higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution. pH 7 is neutral.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using a pH probe instead of universal indicator?
options: It changes the pH of the solution less
It gives a precise numerical value without judging a colour
It does not need to be rinsed
markScheme: 1 mark: it gives a precise / numerical value (without judging a colour)
questions.explanation: A pH probe gives a reading to one or two decimal places. Universal indicator gives an approximate value and depends on how someone judges the colour. Probes must be rinsed between readings.

questions.question: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added a little at a time to sodium hydroxide solution until the acid is in excess. How does the pH change?
options: It rises from about 1 to about 13
It falls from about 13, drops quickly through 7, and ends below 7
It falls from about 13 and stops at exactly 7
markScheme: 1 mark: it falls from a high pH, changes rapidly through 7 and ends below 7
questions.explanation: The starting solution is alkaline (high pH). As acid is added, OH⁻ ions are used up. At neutralisation the pH changes very quickly through 7, and with excess acid the pH is below 7.

questions.question: Universal indicator turns yellow when added to a solution. What is the most likely pH of the solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6
questions.explanation: Yellow shows a weakly acidic solution, about pH 5 to 6. pH 1 would be red, pH 8 blue-green or blue, and pH 12 purple.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide solution was added to hydrochloric acid and the pH measured:
Volume of NaOH (cm³): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
pH: 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 7.0, 12.0, 12.3
What volume of sodium hydroxide solution was needed to make the solution neutral?
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 cm³
questions.explanation: Neutral means pH 7. The table shows pH 7.0 when 20 cm³ of sodium hydroxide had been added.

questions.question:
Use the data below to calculate the overall increase in pH during the experiment.
Volume of NaOH (cm³): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
pH: 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 7.0, 12.0, 12.3
questions.explanation: Final pH − starting pH = 12.3 − 1.0 = 11.3. pH has no units.

questions.question: A student repeated a neutralisation three times. The volumes of alkali needed to reach pH 7 were 19.8 cm³, 20.2 cm³ and 20.0 cm³. Calculate the mean volume.
questions.explanation: Add the three volumes (60.0 cm³) and divide by 3 to get 20.0 cm³.

questions.question: 25 cm³ of an acid is exactly neutralised by 20 cm³ of an alkali. Calculate the volume of the same alkali needed to neutralise 60 cm³ of the same acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8 cm³ of alkali per cm³ of acid (or 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4)
questions.explanation: The volume of alkali is proportional to the volume of acid. 60 cm³ is 2.4 times 25 cm³, so 2.4 × 20 = 48 cm³ of alkali are needed.

questions.question: One antacid tablet neutralises 15 cm³ of a sample of stomach acid. What is the smallest whole number of tablets needed to neutralise 100 cm³ of this acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: round up to 7 tablets
questions.explanation: 6 tablets would only neutralise 90 cm³, leaving some acid. Since you cannot take part of a tablet, you round up to 7.

questions.question: State the range of pH values for an acidic solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: less than 7 (from 0 up to below 7)
questions.explanation: Acids have pH values below 7. The lower the value, the more acidic.

questions.question: Name two ways of measuring the pH of a solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: universal indicator / wide range indicator (solution or paper)
1 mark: pH probe / pH meter / data logger
questions.explanation: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from its colour; a pH probe gives a numerical reading.

questions.question: Describe how to use universal indicator to find the approximate pH of a solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: add a few drops of universal indicator to a sample of the solution (or dip universal indicator paper in it)
1 mark: compare the colour with a pH colour chart to read the pH
questions.explanation: The colour must be matched to the chart supplied with the indicator. Using a white tile behind the test tube makes the colour easier to see.

questions.question: A solution has a pH of 12. State whether it is acidic, neutral or alkaline, and name the ion that causes this.
markScheme: 1 mark: alkaline
1 mark: hydroxide ions / OH⁻
questions.explanation: pH above 7 is alkaline. Alkaline solutions contain hydroxide ions.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between an acid and an alkali.
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
1 mark: state symbols (aq), (aq), (l)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine to form water molecules.

questions.question: Sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid. Explain why Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are not shown in the ionic equation for neutralisation.
markScheme: 1 mark: they do not change / are spectator ions / stay in solution (as the salt)
questions.explanation: Only H⁺ and OH⁻ react. The sodium and chloride ions remain dissolved and make up the salt sodium chloride.

questions.question: A gardener mixes some soil with distilled water and adds universal indicator. It turns orange. Most vegetables grow best at about pH 6.5 to 7. Interpret the result and suggest what the gardener should do.
markScheme: 1 mark: the soil is acidic (about pH 3 to 4)
1 mark: add a base such as lime (calcium hydroxide / calcium carbonate) to neutralise it / raise the pH
questions.explanation: Orange indicates a weakly acidic pH below the ideal range. A base neutralises the acid and raises the pH towards 7.

questions.question: Hydrochloric acid with potassium hydroxide, and nitric acid with sodium hydroxide, have the same ionic equation. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: all acids provide H⁺ ions and all alkalis provide OH⁻ ions, which react to form water (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O)
1 mark: the other ions (K⁺, Cl⁻, Na⁺, NO₃⁻) do not react / are spectator ions
questions.explanation: The only change in every acid and alkali neutralisation is H⁺ and OH⁻ forming water. The other ions only decide which salt is left in solution.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show how the pH changes as sodium hydroxide solution is added to 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid. Include the expected results and explain them in terms of ions.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid into a beaker or conical flask using a measuring cylinder or pipette; measure the starting pH with a calibrated pH probe (or universal indicator, comparing to a colour chart); add sodium hydroxide solution from a burette in small portions (e.g. 5 cm³, smaller near neutral); swirl or stir after each addition and record the pH; continue until the pH stops changing (e.g. 40 cm³ added); rinse the probe with distilled water before use; wear eye protection; expected results: starts at low pH (about 1), rises slowly, then changes rapidly through pH 7 at neutralisation, then levels off at a high pH (about 12 to 13); explanation: the acid contains H⁺ ions; OH⁻ ions from the alkali react with H⁺ to form water (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O); at pH 7 all the H⁺ ions have reacted; after that, extra OH⁻ ions make the solution alkaline.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear method with measurements and a way of recording pH, a correct description of the pH changes and an explanation in terms of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): workable method and some correct description of the pH changes, with limited ionic explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic idea such as adding alkali to acid and measuring pH, with little detail.
questions.explanation: The pH tells you which ion is in excess: below 7 means H⁺ ions remain; above 7 means OH⁻ ions are in excess; at 7 they have exactly reacted.

questions.question:
Hydrochloric acid was added in portions to 20 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution:
Volume of acid (cm³): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
pH: 13.0, 12.8, 12.5, 12.0, 7.0, 2.0, 1.6
Describe the trend in the data and explain the changes in pH in terms of ions.
markScheme: Indicative content: pH starts high (13.0) because the solution contains many OH⁻ ions; pH falls slowly from 13.0 to 12.0 over the first 15 cm³ as H⁺ ions from the acid react with OH⁻ ions to form water; the pH drops sharply between 15 cm³ and 25 cm³, passing pH 7 at 20 cm³ when all the OH⁻ ions have reacted (neutralisation); after 20 cm³ there are excess H⁺ ions so the solution becomes acidic and the pH levels off at about 1.6; H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): trend described using data, with the neutral point identified and changes explained using H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description such as the pH decreases, with little use of data or ions.
questions.explanation: This is the reverse of adding alkali to acid. The steep part of the curve is where the ion in excess switches from OH⁻ to H⁺.

questions.question: Compare the use of universal indicator and a pH probe to measure the pH of a solution.
markScheme: Indicative content: both measure pH on the 0 to 14 scale; universal indicator is cheap, quick and easy to use; it gives an approximate pH (to the nearest whole number); it relies on matching a colour to a chart, which is subjective and hard for colour-blind people or with coloured solutions; a pH probe gives a precise numerical reading (to one or two decimal places); it can record continuously with a data logger; it is more expensive and must be calibrated with buffer solutions and rinsed between readings.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison with advantages and disadvantages of both methods.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one method, for example a probe is more accurate.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs points about both methods, ideally linked: indicator is approximate and subjective; the probe is precise and objective but needs calibration.

questions.question: A solution of pH 2 is mixed with a solution of pH 12. The final mixture has pH 7. Which statement explains this?
options: The H⁺ ions and OH⁻ ions reacted in equal amounts to form water
The water diluted both solutions to pH 7
All of the ions in both solutions reacted to form a precipitate
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺ and OH⁻ ions reacted in equal amounts to form water
questions.explanation: The mixture is neutral because the amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻ were exactly equal, so neither is in excess. pH values do not simply average, and dilution alone cannot make a solution neutral.
